title: An Interface and Algorithms for Authenticated Encryption
summary: Defines algorithms for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD), plus a uniform interface and an IANA registry for them. This lets applications treat such ciphers as interchangeable and encourages reuse of crypto code. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: One lock that both hides your message and proves it was not changed. This makes a common way to use many of those locks, so programs can swap them easily.

subtitle: One interface for ciphers that hide data and prove it was not changed, plus a registry and four AES-based algorithms.

tldr.problem: Applications usually need both secrecy and tamper detection, and combining a cipher with a separate message authentication code is easy to get wrong and ties each application to particular algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5116 defines a single interface for Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (a key, a nonce, plaintext and associated data in, ciphertext out), guidance on nonces, a registry of algorithms, and four AES-GCM and AES-CCM algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Applications can treat AEAD algorithms as interchangeable and name them with one identifier. The RFC is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

facts.label: Algorithms defined
facts.value: 4 (AES-128 and AES-256, each with GCM and CCM)

today: RFC 5116 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the AEAD interface, the nonce guidance and the four algorithms in the registry.

sections.title: Why Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
Authenticated encryption provides confidentiality for the plaintext and also a way to check its integrity and authenticity. Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) adds the ability to check the integrity and authenticity of some associated data that is not encrypted.

Many applications used an encryption method and a Message Authentication Code (MAC) together, each with an independent key. The idea of providing both services with a single cryptoalgorithm has become accepted. The RFC argues that an AEAD algorithm can be analyzed independently of its use in an application. That frees the designer from worrying about the order of authentication and encryption or the security of a particular cipher and MAC combination, and the interface needs only one key and one algorithm identifier.

Implementers gain too: a simpler interface is easier to test, and a hardware module that supports it can accelerate any application that uses it, even ones not yet designed. The RFC does not cover protocol issues such as anti-replay or access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of buying one lock to hide a letter and a different seal to show nobody opened it, you use one gadget that does both jobs. That is simpler and harder to mess up.

sections.title: The AEAD Interface
sections.content:
An AEAD algorithm has two operations, working on octet strings. Authenticated encryption takes four inputs: a secret key K, a nonce N, a plaintext P and associated data A. It outputs a ciphertext C that is at least as long as the plaintext, or an indication that the encryption could not be performed. The key must be uniformly random or pseudorandom, and its length is between 1 and 255 octets and fixed for each algorithm.

The associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. For a network protocol it might hold addresses, ports, sequence numbers or version numbers, fields that must stay readable but should not be forgeable. When the plaintext is empty, the algorithm acts as a MAC on A. The key must never be copied into the other inputs.

Authenticated decryption takes K, N, A and C and returns either the plaintext or the special symbol FAIL meaning the inputs are not authentic. If an input is outside an implementation's supported lengths, it MUST return an error and MUST NOT output any other information, so partial data is never returned.

The RFC does not fix an encoding for the inputs and outputs. It does advise placing the ciphertext after any data needed to build the other decryption inputs, for example nonce before ciphertext in a packet, which helps hardware implementations. Applications MUST NOT assume any structure in the ciphertext.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the machine a key, a one-time number, your secret message, and some labels that stay visible. It gives back a scrambled message. To undo it, it checks the seal first, and if the seal is wrong it says FAIL instead of giving anything back.

sections.title: Using Nonces Safely
sections.content:
The nonce is the part applications most often get wrong. For any one key, every nonce passed to encryption MUST be distinct, unless every nonce is zero-length. If an application cannot guarantee uniqueness, it MUST use a zero-length nonce, which suits randomized or stateful algorithms. Otherwise the nonce SHOULD be twelve octets long.

The RFC recommends building nonces from a Fixed field followed by a Counter field. The counter starts at zero (or another value) and increases by one, and the Fixed field is constant for a device. If several devices share one key, each MUST use a distinct Fixed field. Implementations SHOULD support 12-octet nonces with a four-octet counter. When part of the nonce is implicit (for example inferred from a position on disk), the Fixed field is split into Fixed-Common and Fixed-Distinct, and the Fixed-Distinct and Counter parts MUST be carried explicitly. The RFC says this is how GCM and CCM in IPsec ESP build their nonces.

Long-lived keys need the nonce stored in non-volatile memory with checkpointing, for instance by storing a value several steps ahead. Changing the key is another way to avoid nonce trouble.

When the associated data or plaintext is built from several elements, it must be unambiguously parseable without unauthenticated data, for example by including the length of a variable-length string. The RFC's worked example expresses AES-GCM in ESP this way.
sections.plainLanguage: The one-time number must never be used twice with the same key, like a ticket number that only works once. Giving each machine its own ticket prefix, then counting up, keeps them from ever clashing.

sections.title: Requirements on Algorithm Specifications
sections.content:
Any algorithm that plugs into this interface must meet a few rules. It MUST accept only keys of one fixed length, K_LEN, and MUST NOT require special key structure. It MUST accept plaintexts from zero up to P_MAX octets and associated data up to A_MAX octets, and both limits MUST be larger than zero and SHOULD be at least 65,536 octets, a typical upper limit for network packets.

It MUST accept nonces between N_MIN and N_MAX octets, and SHOULD accept twelve octets. The specification must also state the largest ciphertext, C_MAX, and how plaintext length relates to ciphertext length, and that relation MUST NOT depend on outside parameters such as tag length. Specifications SHOULD describe what happens on nonce reuse and reference a security analysis.

An algorithm is randomized if it uses a random source during encryption (decryption stays deterministic), and stateful if it keeps state between encryptions. Both kinds MAY have an N_MAX of zero and SHOULD say so.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who wants to add a new lock to the family must write down its key size, how big a message it can take, and what goes wrong if the one-time number is reused.

sections.title: The Four Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 5116 defines four algorithms: two based on AES in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and two on AES in Counter with CBC-MAC mode (CCM), each with a 128-bit and a 256-bit key. All use a 16-octet authentication tag appended to the ciphertext, so the ciphertext is exactly 16 octets longer than the plaintext, and all use a 12-octet nonce. The 256-bit variants differ only in K_LEN of 32 octets and in using AES-256.

The RFC is blunt about nonce reuse. With GCM, reusing a nonce with the same key for different plaintexts undermines confidentiality and all of the authenticity protection, because an attacker can recover the XOR of the two plaintexts and the internal hash key, which makes forgeries trivial. GCM should only be used when nonce uniqueness can be assured. With CCM, reuse costs confidentiality, because the XOR of the two plaintexts can be reconstructed. Reusing a nonce in decryption is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ready-made locks, two kinds, each in a normal and a stronger size. All of them add the same size seal, and all of them break badly if you reuse the one-time number.

sections.title: The IANA AEAD Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains an AEAD Registry so algorithms can be named by number. Each entry has a short name starting with AEAD, a positive number assigned by IANA (using the smallest available), and a reference to a specification that fully defines the algorithm and provides test cases. Additions need an RFC or another permanent, readily available reference. Submitters SHOULD have requests reviewed by the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group.

Numbers from 32,768 to 65,535 are reserved for private use. The four algorithms in this RFC took numbers 1 to 4. A registration is not an endorsement of the algorithm's security.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry is a phone book of locks. Each lock gets a name and a number so two programs can just say lock number 1 and know what they mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
AEAD makes some parts of cryptographic design easier, but strong security is still difficult. AEAD algorithms do nothing for key generation or key management. Algorithms that rely on distinct nonces may be wrong for some applications, so designers should understand the nonce requirements.

A software implementation running in a virtual machine could reuse a nonce if the VM is rolled back to an earlier state. Applications are encouraged to document that risk. The RFC adds that an attacker able to trigger a rollback may already have subverted the system, and that mitigations remain an area of active research. Finally, the perceived security of an algorithm can degrade over time through cryptanalytic advances or falling computation costs.
sections.plainLanguage: A good lock does not help if you lose the key or reuse the one-time number. And locks can become easier to pick as the years go by.

sections.title: Testing and Future Algorithms
sections.content:
A randomized encryption algorithm cannot be tested with fixed input and output pairs. The RFC suggests testing decryption directly, since it is deterministic, and testing encryption by encrypting, decrypting and comparing with the original plaintext.

The four algorithms were chosen because standards had already adopted them. The RFC calls it an open question which others to add, and notes the trade-off between admitting useful algorithms and limiting the registry's size. It suggests that a generic encrypt-then-MAC composition, such as CBC with HMAC-SHA1 or AES CMAC, may be worth defining.
sections.plainLanguage: Some locks pick a random pattern each time, so you test them by locking and unlocking and checking the message comes back the same.
